opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say we're still far from done, maybe somewhere in the early chapters of a long book. With Taichi, the part I feel good about is the core idea: you can write high-performance parallel code, for physical simulation, graphics, and so on, in something that feels like Python, and the compiler handles the hard parts. Seeing people around the world use it in research, in courses, in their own creative projects, that's very rewarding. It tells me the direction is right.

But "complete" is a high bar. A programming language or infrastructure project only really succeeds when it becomes something people rely on without thinking about it, like a utility. We're not there yet. There's still a lot to do on stability, documentation, the ecosystem, and making the developer experience smooth enough that someone who isn't a graphics or compiler person can just pick it up and be productive.

With the company side, the way I assess progress is less about technical milestones and more about whether we're creating real value for users. Are people coming back? Are they building things they couldn't build before? In research you can publish a paper and call it done. In a startup the feedback is much more brutal and much more honest. The market tells you whether you're right.

So my personal metric is roughly this: each year, am I solving a harder and more important problem than the year before, and is the team learning faster than the problem is growing? If yes, I think we're on track, even if the destination still looks far away. And to be honest, I kind of like that it's far away. If it were easy, it probably wouldn't be worth spending ten years on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses creating user value and using market feedback, but does not identify product-market fit as the halfway milestone for MatchU.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention an IPO as the milestone completing MatchU’s remaining half.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd say we're still early on both, and I try to be careful not to overstate where things are.

With Taichi, I'm genuinely proud of what the community built. It started as my PhD project at MIT, essentially a way to make high-performance graphics and physical simulation programmable in Python, without having to hand-write CUDA kernels for every new idea. Open-sourcing it and watching it grow to hundreds of thousands of users, people doing fluid simulation, soft-body dynamics, and research that would have been painful before, that felt like a real milestone. But if you ask whether it's "complete," no. A programming language is never really done. There are always gaps in the compiler, platforms we don't support well enough, and the hardest problem, which is keeping a vibrant open-source community healthy over many years. I'd call it a meaningful accomplishment that is still unfinished.

MatchU is much younger, so I'd be even more humble there. The idea is to take all of that simulation knowledge, especially cloth and garments, and turn it into something ordinary people can use, letting you see how clothes actually fit and move on your body before you buy them. The technical problem is harder than it looks. Real-time, physically plausible cloth on arbitrary bodies, running on consumer devices, with fabric that looks right rather than merely plausible, that's a serious engineering challenge. We've made progress on the simulation core, and early users like it, but product-market fit is a different kind of problem from compiler design. You can't just benchmark your way to it.

So how do I assess progress? I think of it as two layers. The technical foundation, I'm fairly confident about. We know how to make fast, accurate simulation. The question for the next few years is whether we can translate that into something that changes how people shop and how clothing gets designed. If that happens, then I'd be comfortable calling it a major accomplishment. Until then, I'd say we're maybe a third of the way, with a lot of the hard, unglamorous work still ahead. And frankly, that's the part I enjoy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses product-market fit as a challenge and says MatchU would be a major accomplishment if it changes shopping or clothing design, but it does not identify achieving product-market fit as the halfway milestone.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention an IPO as the milestone that would complete MatchU’s remaining half.

astra-6.text: I think it’s still too early to call them complete, major accomplishments. For both Taichi and MatchU, I’d judge progress by whether we’re solving real problems and creating something people find useful. There’s a difference between building something technically interesting and making a lasting impact. I’m encouraged by the work, but there’s still a lot to do before I’d say we’ve achieved that.

sol-6.1.text: I think both are still works in progress. With Taichi, we’ve made meaningful progress in making high-performance programming more accessible, but there’s still a lot to do before I’d call it a complete accomplishment. With MatchU, I’d apply the same standard: does it solve a real problem, and do people find it useful? For me, the milestone isn’t simply building something or launching it. It’s seeing it deliver lasting value.
